Libya Launches National Integrated Project to Reduce Violence Against Children.

Government-led project brings together families, schools, services and communities around a shared national approach to prevention and protection.

TRIPOLI, 26 November 2026 – The Government of Libya today launched the National Integrated Project for Reducing Violence Against Children, marking an important step towards strengthening prevention, protection and support for children across the country.

Led by the Ministry of Education, together with the Ministries of Social Affairs and Health, and with technical support from UNICEF, the initiative brings national institutions together around a common goal: helping children grow and learn in safe, supportive environments.

During the ceremony, H.E the Minister of Education, Mohamed Al-Qariou "Protecting children from violence is a national responsibility that begins with prevention." Through this project, we are uniting the efforts of families, schools and national institutions under a shared approach that places children's safety, dignity and well-being at the heart of our work. Our commitment is to turn these efforts into sustainable practices that guarantee every child a safe and supportive environment in which to learn and grow.

National evidence has reinforced the need for a more comprehensive and sustainable approach to prevent violence against children. Statistical findings published by the Ministry of Planning have highlighted concerning levels of violence, underscoring the importance of moving beyond responding after violence occurs towards earlier prevention and more positive practices within families, schools and communities.

“A child’s sense of safety is built in everyday moments; in how they are spoken to at home, how they are treated at school, and whether they know that someone will listen when they need help,” said Abdullahi Mohammed, UNICEF Representative in Libya. “By working together, we can turn that sense of safety into everyday reality. UNICEF remains committed to supporting national efforts to strengthen prevention, protection and care for every child in Libya.”

The development and preparation of the project have been supported through contributions from the European Union, the Kingdom of the Netherlands and GIZ, alongside UNICEF. This support has contributed to the technical development and adaptation of the programme, capacity building, and readiness for implementation.

Following the launch, the project will move into its next phase of nationwide implementation across 19 municipalities in Libya. Through a municipal-level cascade model, the project aims to build a future network of approximately 5,000 facilitators equipped to support delivery at community level.
The launch therefore represents a beginning rather than an endpoint. The longer-term goal is to embed effective violence-prevention approaches within national and local systems, supported by trained personnel, safeguarding and referral mechanisms, community engagement, monitoring and sustained government ownership.

items.title: Yemen: Calling for Collective Action and Resource Mobilization to Scale Up the Urgent Humanitarian Response
items.author: Life for Relief and Development
items.content:
Country: Yemen
Source: Life for Relief and Development
  • 369,000 internally displaced people need essential humanitarian assistance to survive.
  • Taiz and Lahj are among the leading governorates of origin for displaced families, requiring intensified relief efforts.
  • Women and children are among the groups most severely affected by the conflict.

Internal displacement continues across Yemen amid the escalating consequences of the conflict and mounting humanitarian pressures on affected families. According to the International Organization for Migration (IOM) Yemen report released this month, 369,012 people, representing 61,502 households, have been displaced this year.

The report indicates that Taiz was the leading governorate of origin for displaced people during the monitoring period, accounting for 48% of the total, followed by Lahj at 45% and Al Hudaydah at 3%. The remaining 4% came from several other governorates, including Marib, Al Dhale'e, Ibb, Aden, Abyan, Sana'a, Hajjah, Shabwah, Al Bayda, Al Jawf, Al Mahwit, Dhamar, and Hadramout.

Women and Children Among the Most Severely Affected

In response to this escalating humanitarian crisis, numerous relief organizations have launched initiatives to support those in need. To gain a closer understanding of conditions on the ground, we spoke with Eng. Mabrouk Shubail, Director of LIFE for Relief and Development's office in Yemen, about the humanitarian situation, the challenges facing displaced families, and the difficulties confronting humanitarian workers.

The following is our interview:

To begin, could you explain the reality of the humanitarian situation in Yemen following the escalation of political tensions in the region?

Certainly. According to the United Nations' 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan and UNICEF, approximately 22.3 million people in Yemen require humanitarian assistance, including 10.95 million women and girls in need of assistance and protection.

Approximately 2.2 million children under the age of five are suffering from acute malnutrition, while 1.3 million pregnant and breastfeeding women are at risk of malnutrition. More than 7 million children also face increased protection risks, while approximately 4.5 million children have been deprived of education. These figures reflect the extensive humanitarian consequences of the conflict, particularly for women and children.

Protection assessments reveal specific risks facing women and children. Why are these groups particularly vulnerable?

In general, women and children living in conflict and displacement settings face overlapping humanitarian, health, psychological, and social risks. Their suffering extends far beyond losing their homes or fleeing areas of active fighting. It also includes threats to their physical safety, restricted access to essential services, and exposure to various forms of violence, exploitation, and harassment in unsafe shelter environments.

As conditions in Yemen continue to deteriorate, an increasing number of households are being headed by women. Repeated displacement further intensifies their suffering, particularly due to the lack of adequate shelter, overcrowding in available accommodation, and limited living space.

Additional health risks arise from chronic illnesses affecting some family members, the spread of communicable diseases, and gaps in vaccination coverage. There is also a critical shortage of psychological first aid and crisis counseling services, which are essential early interventions for protecting vulnerable populations.

How do you assess the relief needs of displaced families?

As the humanitarian situation in Yemen deteriorates following the renewed conflict, many families have lost their homes and possessions. This has increased the urgent need for humanitarian interventions that provide shelter to displaced and affected households, improve their living conditions, ease their suffering, and strengthen their ability to cope with the consequences of displacement.

The Executive Unit for the Management of Displacement Camps, operating under the Yemeni Prime Minister's Office, has identified several essential humanitarian needs facing displaced families that require urgent intervention. These include:

  • Food Assistance: Providing food and essential supplies to affected households.
  • Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH): Ensuring access to safe water, hygiene supplies, and adequate sanitation facilities.
  • Healthcare: Providing displaced people with essential medical services and healthcare.
  • Shelter and Accommodation: Supplying suitable housing and shelter materials to protect families from harsh living conditions.
  • Protection: Strengthening protection measures for displaced populations, particularly the most vulnerable groups.
  • Livelihoods and Cash Assistance: Supporting families in restoring their ability to meet their basic living needs.

In light of these indicators, the report issued an urgent appeal to mobilize funding and resources and strengthen operational capacities, with the aim of expanding the coordinated humanitarian response and providing the necessary assistance to displaced households.

How can humanitarian workers determine priorities when dealing with such a massive number of people in need?

The fundamental responsibility of humanitarian workers is to provide people with the basic necessities required for survival. The expanding scale of displacement, with affected families spread across ten governorates and 59 districts, makes stronger coordination among relief organizations and intensified joint efforts essential to meeting growing needs and ensuring that assistance reaches the most vulnerable households.

We have made considerable efforts to identify areas that have not yet received humanitarian assistance, assess the most vulnerable cases, and determine their specific needs.

Our planned assistance in Taiz and Lahj includes support for displacement camps and the provision of essential household items. These supplies include mattresses and foam pillows, large sleeping mattresses, floor mats, two-burner gas stoves and cooking utensils, dining plates, two-gallon water containers, 20-liter water buckets, and 25-liter gas cylinders.

As an initial step, we have worked to support approximately 600 families and are currently identifying additional highly vulnerable households to expand the scope of our assistance.

As Director of LIFE for Relief and Development's office in Yemen, what challenges are you facing?

Some of the challenges exceed what a single relief organization can address independently and require collective action and cooperation among all stakeholders. The scale of need is enormous due to the growing number of people affected by the widening conflict. Reaching the poorest and most vulnerable households requires coordinated efforts, as does reviewing and verifying beneficiary lists to exclude individuals who have not been directly affected and ensuring that assistance is delivered directly to beneficiaries in the field.

Nevertheless, we believe these challenges can be addressed.

LIFE has been operating in Yemen for 34 years. This longstanding presence has enabled us to develop an in-depth understanding of the country's conditions, the nature of humanitarian needs, and the challenges facing affected communities.

We therefore work simultaneously across different areas through our teams deployed in several governorates. These teams coordinate closely to accelerate needs assessments and ensure the timely implementation of relief activities.

For more information:

https://lifeusa.org/#social-media

items.title: DR Congo: Ebola disease survivors share their stories
items.author: Médecins Sans Frontières
items.content:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: Médecins Sans Frontières

Christine and her ten-year-old son, Jérémie, fell sick with Ebola disease after attending a funeral in September.

“Soon after getting home, I started to get headaches,” says Christine. “The next day, it got worse.”

The pair visited a local hospital, but as their symptoms – vomiting and diarrhoea – got worse, they were eventually transferred to the Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) Ebola treatment centre (ETC) in Beni, North Kivu province, Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

Medical staff feared they would not make it.

In the more than six months since the Ebola disease outbreak was declared in DRC, close to 12,000 people have been infected, according to the Ministry of Health. The true figure is certainly higher. Around half of the people who are infected die from the disease.

One of the reasons that the mortality rate is so high is that many people seek care only when the disease has already reached an advanced stage.

“We can do more to increase the chances of survival of patients who come as soon as they experience symptoms,” says Dr Louis Vala Moweni, medical coordinator for MSF’s Ebola response. “But many arrive too late.”

Ebola disease can progress rapidly and lead to severe complications. This is why patients should seek medical care as soon as they develop early symptoms, such as fever and headaches.

Although the outbreak was officially declared in May, many people still hesitate to come to ETCs because of fear, misinformation, and distrust towards the Ebola response.

“I thought that no one makes it out of here alive and that doctors and nurses kill people,” says Ghislaine, another survivor recently discharged from the Beni ETC. “I was surprised to experience the opposite.”

For Dr Moweni, high levels of fear in the community are understandable.

“At the beginning of the outbreak, people saw medical staff arriving in full personal protective equipment (PPE) and taking patients away,” he says. “Regrettably, many people died. We need to acknowledge that this instils fear in communities.”

However, thanks to their testimonies, survivors are now helping to counter rumours and strengthen communities’ trust in health teams.

“Seeing survivors walk out of ETCs alive, and hearing what they have to say is one of the best ways to combat that fear,” says Dr Moweni.

In Mongbwalu, Ituri province, where the outbreak originated, there were significant fears when we began our response in May.

“People were dying in cascades,” recalls Deogracias Kasereka, a pastor from the town, who later fell ill after presiding over a funeral.

His daughter, who had worked on a previous outbreak, encouraged him to get tested for Ebola disease.

“At that time, people were afraid, because going to the hospital meant death,” says Pastor Kasereka. “But I made up my mind. I said to myself, ‘if I must die of Ebola, then I will die. And if I can be cured, then I will be cured’. So, I decided to go.”

After testing positive, the pastor was treated at the ETC and, in June, became the first patient in the town to recover from Ebola disease. Patients started to arrive at earlier stages of infection and mortality rates among them began to fall.

“When they saw me alive, it encouraged many people,” he says. “They had said, ‘Even the pastor will die’. But seeing me return gave people hope.”

“From the day I was discharged, I began awareness-raising in the community,” says Pastor Kasereka. “I went directly into the church communities to speak to people. Since then, I have continued this work, even in schools.”

While attitudes towards the response are changing in some areas, some survivors still face acute stigma.

“There is often a paradox in the experience of survivors,” says Dr Moweni. “While they want to put their experience to the benefit of their communities and contribute to the fight against the outbreak, they can also become victims of stigma and attacks. This adds to their suffering at a time when they are still recovering from the disease.”

When Francine, who fell ill with Ebola disease after losing one of her children to the disease, was discharged from the Mongbwalu ETC in October, she found that the community had burned down her home — fearing it to be contaminated.

“I do not want to speak with them anymore,” says Francine. “I do not know how I will survive.”

At a survivor clinic supported by MSF, and adjacent to Mongbwalu ETC, patients receive medical and psychological support through individual consultations. MSF pays for transport costs to help survivors living far away reach the clinic.

“Some survivors are feared in their communities,” says Jean-Paul Wayotho Pariu, an MSF health promoter. “We advise them how to reintegrate and how to avoid shame and feel at ease. The perception of this disease makes many people see it as shameful.”

Despite the challenges, patients who survive Ebola disease also feel great relief.

“I am happy to return home,” says Christine, on the day of her release, alongside Jérémie, after more than a month of treatment. “In the ETC, I spent the whole time thinking about my family and my children.”

Her message to the community is clear: “If other people feel sick, they should come to the ETC and not stay at home. They [healthcare staff] will look after you.”

items.title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 26 November 2026\
items.author: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
items.content:
Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

Key Highlights

  • At least 600 aid workers have been killed in Gaza since October 2023, including 13 since the ceasefire was announced, following the killing of an UNRWA staff member in an Israeli strike on 23 November.
  • The World Health Organization reports 692 suspected meningitis cases between 1 October and 23 November, following a sharp increase in cases in mid- and late October, with infants under one year of age accounting for most cases.
  • Essential winter supplies in Gaza cost over eight times as much when procured locally as when procured internationally, while only 35 per cent of minimum winter shelter response requirements are funded, according to the Norwegian Refugee Council.
  • Child protection partners in Gaza report increasing child labour and hazardous responsibilities, exposing children to exploitation, explosive remnants of war and further disruptions to education.
  • According to the Logistics Cluster, 405 trucks carrying humanitarian supplies were offloaded on the Israeli side of Kerem Shalom Crossing between 16 and 23 November, a six per cent decrease compared with the preceding week.
  • Intensified movement restrictions, settler violence and demolitions in Masafer Yatta, in southern Hebron governorate, are severely disrupting access to essential services and livelihoods, heightening the risk of further displacement.
  • Israeli authorities demolish 79 Palestinian-owned structures across the West Bank in one week, including all remaining structures in Khirbet Samra in the northern Jordan Valley.
  • The Humanitarian Country Team calls for urgent protection of Palestinian olive harvesters amid unprecedented levels of harvest-related settler violence.
  • A US$40 million allocation from the occupied Palestinian territory Humanitarian Fund was launched. The 2026 Flash Appeal remains only 35.5 per cent funded.

West Bank

The reporting period is 17 to 23 November 2026 unless otherwise specified.

Israeli forces' operations, settler violence, demolitions and movement restrictions continued to drive displacement and undermine Palestinian livelihoods and access to essential services across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem. In herding and farming communities, particularly in Masafer Yatta and the Jordan Valley, the combined impact of violence, access restrictions and the destruction of essential infrastructure is increasingly undermining communities' ability to remain on their land.

During the reporting period, an Israeli settlement guard shot and killed a Palestinian man near Dura al Qar' (Ramallah). According to the Israeli military, a settlement security coordinator opened fire when two Palestinian men approached Beit El settlement, killing one, while the other was arrested. The Israeli military stated that the incident was under investigation.

Overall, 47 Palestinians, including six children, were injured during the reporting period, of whom eight were injured by Israeli settlers and 39 by Israeli forces. Twelve Palestinians (26 per cent) were injured in the context of settler attacks, including three in incidents related to the olive harvest. Operations by Israeli forces displaced 11 Palestinians, while demolitions displaced another 67.

The cumulative impact of violence, demolitions, displacement and movement restrictions is also taking a toll on Palestinians' mental health and psychosocial well-being. According to a report published by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) on 19 November, exposure to violence accounted for approximately 70 per cent of recorded reasons for seeking mental health care from MSF teams in the West Bank between October 2022 and April 2026. The report also found that anxiety and depression-related symptoms accounted for about two thirds of reported mental health conditions. These needs are compounded by restrictions on access to health services and humanitarian assistance.

Since the beginning of October, intensified movement restrictions imposed by the Israeli authorities, alongside recurrent settler attacks, have increasingly undermined access to essential services, livelihoods and humanitarian assistance in Masafer Yatta, in southern Hebron governorate. Restrictions on vehicle access to the area designated by the Israeli authorities as “Firing Zone 918” have severely disrupted deliveries of food, water and animal fodder, as well as access to health and education services. These arrangements are insufficient to accommodate daily schooling, emergency medical needs and regular deliveries of essential supplies, including water.

According to the Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) Cluster, water trucking operations serving more than 1,500 Palestinians across 10 of the 12 remaining communities within the Israeli-designated firing zone in Masafer Yatta remain severely constrained. The programme was initiated in late April following settler attacks in January and February 2026 that severed the communities’ water supply network, which partners remain unable to restore. The programme was recently expanded to cover three additional communities outside the firing zone. Following limited deliveries in November, Israeli settlers reportedly seized a water truck and physically assaulted its driver on 14 November near Isfai al Fouqa. Although residents and the village council subsequently retrieved the truck, deliveries were further disrupted. So far in November, limited quantities of water have reached only three communities inside the firing zone and two outside it.

Between 1 October and 23 November, Israeli forces confiscated at least 18 Palestinian-owned vehicles, including agricultural tractors, private vehicles and a vehicle belonging to a local organization. According to the village council, Israeli authorities had verbally communicated through the Palestinian District Coordination and Liaison Office that vehicles operating within the designated area, except those belonging to the Palestinian Ministry of Education, would be subject to confiscation. The closure of a road gate near Carmel settlement on 23 October has further restricted movement along key routes serving at least 5,800 Palestinians south of Yatta. The restrictions also coincide with the lambing season, a critical period for herding communities, with disruptions to fodder supplies threatening livestock health and productivity and the sustainability of household livelihoods.

The area was designated by the Israeli authorities as a firing zone in the 1980s. On 17 June 2025, the Israeli military issued a notice that the area would be used for military training. In conjunction with this announcement, the Israeli Civil Administration issued a planning directive allowing the retroactive dismissal of Palestinian planning applications, further heightening the risk of mass demolitions and displacement. Since 2009, Israeli authorities have demolished 422 Palestinian-owned structures in the firing zone area of Masafer Yatta, including 240 (57 per cent) that had been provided as humanitarian assistance. Nearly a quarter of these structures (97) were demolished in 2026 alone, displacing 118 Palestinians, including 58 children, and otherwise affecting 136 people. Agricultural, livelihood and water and sanitation structures accounted for approximately 60 per cent of all structures demolished this year. Schools, health clinics and other essential civilian infrastructure remain at risk of demolition.

Since January 2023, more than 160 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage have been documented in communities in Masafer Yatta located within the Israeli-designated firing zone, including 41 so far in 2026. Attacks have repeatedly targeted homes, water and electricity infrastructure, livestock, agricultural assets and vehicles used to transport essential supplies and students. In some cases, settlers have subsequently attacked homes belonging to families already displaced, further undermining prospects for return. Since the beginning of 2026, 50 Palestinians, including 29 children, have been displaced due to settler violence and related access restrictions. The combined impact of recurrent demolitions, sustained settler violence, intensified movement restrictions and the erosion of livelihoods is heightening the risk of further displacement.

Protection partners continue to provide legal assistance, including follow-up on vehicle confiscations and access restrictions, alongside psychosocial support, specialized child protection services, gender-based violence prevention and mitigation interventions, cash for protection and protective presence where access allows. Given restrictions on vehicle access, partners are also supporting community-based protection initiatives to identify urgent needs and facilitate referrals, documenting incidents and their humanitarian impact, and raising urgent protection concerns through existing coordination mechanisms.

items.title: The Persecution Continues: Minority Communities Under Sustained Attack in Bangladesh (January - October 2026)
items.author: Human Rights Congress for Bangladesh Minorities
items.content:
Country: Bangladesh
Source: Human Rights Congress for Bangladesh Minorities

Please refer to the attached file.

Between 1 January and 31 October 2026, the Human Rights Congress for Bangladesh Minorities (HRCBM) documented 1,445 incidents affecting religious, ethnic, and Indigenous minority communities across all 64 districts and eight administrative divisions of Bangladesh. The Persecution Continues combines national and district-level statistics with representative cases to examine recurring violence, dispossession, and barriers to justice.

The documented incidents include 286 reported murders and unexplained deaths, 408 attacks on homes, land, and other property, 251 attacks on temples or other religious sites and incidents of religious vandalism, and 30 blasphemy-related incidents across 14 districts. The report also documents missing-person cases, abductions, physical assaults, and sexual violence. These figures are documented minimums. Fear of retaliation, stigma, and barriers to reporting and verification contribute to underreporting, particularly of sexual violence.

The report examines how disputed allegations of religious insult can lead to arrests and retaliation against families and communities, how land grabbing and intimidation can pressure families to leave their homes, and how delays in registering complaints, inadequate investigations, and threats against victims and witnesses can obstruct access to justice. HRCBM calls for equal protection, impartial investigations, effective remedies, and direct participation by affected communities in transitional justice. It identifies patterns that warrant independent examination as possible crimes against humanity.

For journalists, researchers, and human rights practitioners, the report provides monthly trends, district-level tables, case accounts, and an explanation of HRCBM’s verification methodology. It also records selected submissions to national and international institutions and the responses known at publication. Please cite the DOI for the version consulted. The Zenodo record provides access to later versions as corrections, additional corroboration, and case developments become available.

Source: Mixed Migration Centre

In late February 2026, war between the United States and Iran displaced millions within weeks, in a country that already hosted the world’s largest refugee population, with many already at risk of deportation to Afghanistan. Sudan, now the world’s largest displacement crisis, entered its fourth year of war with famine confirmed and a humanitarian appeal completely underfunded. Haiti’s collapse deepened, largely unwatched. The statements and actions by the current US administration continue to shock its traditional allies on the other side of the Atlantic. Russia’s war on Ukraine continues with no end in sight. Transport corridors vital for the world economy, like the Strait of Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb, are strategically blocked. Analysts warn that the AI boom might soon cause another financial crisis, while ever more AI experts and the leading AI companies warn of an existential crisis due to AI. The planet keeps warming past thresholds we once described as limits, with Europeans increasingly experiencing the impact, including an estimated 35,000 excess deaths due to back-to-back heatwaves and near-constant wildfires across the continent, while a large part of the world might need to brace itself for the most severe El Niño ever.

items.title: World: Legal Identity for Displaced People in West and Central Africa - From reform to effective access: turning political commitment into protection outcomes
items.author: Norwegian Refugee Council
items.content:
Countries: World, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Mali, Niger, Nigeria
Source: Norwegian Refugee Council

Please refer to the attached file.

Across West and Central Africa, millions of refugees, internally displaced people and returnees are unable to obtain, replace or recover essential civil documentation. For people affected by displacement, legal identity is not simply an administrative issue. The absence of birth certificates, identity cards and other civil documents can become a humanitarian and protection concern, limiting access to assistance, education, healthcare, livelihoods, freedom of movement and other fundamental rights. It can also prevent displaced people from accessing durable solutions, including return, local integration and the recovery of housing, land and property.

Drawing on research across eight countries in West and Central Africa, this NRC advocacy note examines the barriers displaced populations face in accessing legal identity and documentation.

It calls on governments, donors and humanitarian and development actors to:

  • strengthen civil registration and documentation systems in displacement-affected areas; remove legal, administrative and financial barriers that prevent displaced people from obtaining documentation;
  • integrate legal identity more systematically into humanitarian response plans and durable solutions strategies;
  • and invest in accessible, inclusive and long-term solutions that ensure no displaced person is left without proof of identity and legal existence.

The report highlights practical entry points ranging from mobile registration services and late birth registration procedures to cross-border cooperation, legal assistance, and strengthened support to national civil registration systems.

items.creator: World Health Organization
items.title: WHO and partners sustain lifesaving surgical care as conflict escalates in Yemen
items.author: World Health Organization
items.content:
Country: Yemen
Source: World Health Organization

The interviews with Dr Mustafa Mohammed Munassar, Head of Orthopaedics, and Dr Ahmed Mohammed Saeed Salem, Head of the Intensive Care Unit, at Al-Mansoura General Surgical Hospital (formerly 22 May Hospital), Aden, Yemen, were conducted on 9 November 2026

26 November 2026, Aden, Yemen – Hostilities have intensified across Yemen since the escalation of conflict on 6 August 2026, resulting in increased casualty numbers and large-scale displacement, with Marib, Lahj and Taiz among the areas most affected.

By 16 November 2026, the Health Emergency Operations Centre had recorded 12 779 conflict-related casualties, including 10 519 injuries and 2260 deaths, with 1024 casualties occurring since 8 November. These figures are provisional. Underreporting means the actual toll is likely to be higher.

According to the International Organization for Migration’s Displacement Tracking Matrix, 347 321 people were displaced between 1 August and 14 November, including 18 780 between 8 and 14 November. Lahj and Taiz were the main destinations for those displaced between these dates.

Frontlines have moved through Lahj towards Aden, threatening referral routes and medical supply chains serving key hospitals, placing further pressure on an already overstretched health system. In Taiz, severe shortages of fuel, surgical supplies and anaesthesia medicines are disrupting emergency services, operating theatres and oxygen generation for intensive care units. Al-Mansoura General Surgical Hospital in Aden was receiving 15 to 20 people with conflict-related injuries each day when the interviews were conducted. For many of these patients, timely access to surgery and intensive care can mean the difference between life and death.

Already struggling with shortages of health workers, medical supplies and equipment, the hospital is working around the clock to meet the growing demand for emergency trauma care while continuing to provide essential services to patients with other urgent and chronic conditions.

With funding from the United Nations Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF), the World Health Organization (WHO), in coordination with the Ministry of Public Health and Population, is supporting a specialized surgical team working alongside hospital staff. CERF funding is also enabling WHO to deploy specialized surgical teams to other hospitals in Aden, Abyan and Taiz, helping expand access to lifesaving trauma and surgical services.

“We receive between 15 and 20 people with war injuries every day, and our department performs five to six operations daily,” says Dr Mustafa Mohammed Munassar, Head of Orthopaedics at Al-Mansoura General Surgical Hospital. “The number of wounded arriving at the hospital exceeds its capacity and the current staff.”

Surgical care involves more than the performing of operations. Patients need diagnostic examinations, anaesthesia, medicines, nursing care and monitoring during recovery. Shortages of funding and personnel are making it difficult for the hospital to meet these needs.

The pressure extends to intensive care units, where shortages of trained personnel prevent hospitals from fully using their available resources. Al-Mansoura Hospital has two intensive care units, one with six beds, the other with four. Staffing constraints mean that only the six-bed unit can be used.

“We need medical staff – nurses and doctors – so that we can open the second care unit,” says Dr Ahmed Mohammed Saeed Salem, Head of the Intensive Care Unit.

Without a CT scanner, patients – many of them in critical condition and unable to be easily moved – must be transferred elsewhere for diagnostic examinations. Surgical specialties share a single C-arm imaging device, and shortages of laboratory supplies and essential treatments further compound the challenges facing medical teams.

There is an urgent need for sustained support that combines specialized personnel, essential medical supplies and functioning equipment to ensure patients receive comprehensive care.

WHO support – including the provision of fuel, medical supplies, intravenous fluids and equipment, is helping hospital teams maintain essential services despite the pressures, says Dr Ahmed, and CERF-funded specialized surgical teams are reinforcing the capacity of hospitals to respond to urgent trauma cases.

Among the patients receiving care at Al-Mansoura Hospital was 18-year-old Abdullah Waddah, who needed emergency surgery after a road accident. His experience highlights the importance of maintaining care for everyday emergencies alongside the response to conflict-related injuries.

“The surgery was successful and everything is fine, praise be to God,” he says. “Our brothers the nurses did their best.”

During a visit to the hospital, WHO Representative in Yemen Dr Syed Jaffar Hussain met patients from Taiz and other areas affected by fighting. He highlighted the growing burden on health facilities which must treat people injured in the conflict while continuing to provide care for acute and chronic illnesses in the surrounding communities and displaced populations. As the conflict continues to place additional demands on Yemen's already strained health system, maintaining access to emergency surgical and critical care is essential.

Through CERF funding, WHO is working with national health authorities and health workers to keep lifesaving surgical services available to people affected by the conflict. Sustained investment will be critical to ensuring that hospitals can continue treating the wounded and providing essential care to communities whose needs are growing.

Thanking CERF for its support, Dr Hussain called for continued donor assistance to help health partners sustain the emergency response. “We will be able to save precious lives if we have the means,” he says.

The interviews with Dr Mustafa Mohammed Munassar, Head of Orthopaedics, and Dr Ahmed Mohammed Saeed Salem, Head of the Intensive Care Unit, at Al-Mansoura General Surgical Hospital (formerly 22 May Hospital), Aden, Yemen, were conducted on 9 November 2026
26 November 2026, Aden, Yemen – Hostilities have intensified across Yemen since the escalation of conflict on 6 August 2026, resulting in increased casualty numbers and large-scale displacement, with Marib, Lahj and Taiz among the areas most affected.
By 16 November 2026, the Health Emergency Operations Centre had recorded 12 779 conflict-related casualties, including 10 519 injuries and 2260 deaths, with 1024 casualties occurring since 8 November. These figures are provisional. Underreporting means the actual toll is likely to be higher.
According to the International Organization for Migration’s Displacement Tracking Matrix, 347 321 people were displaced between 1 August and 14 November, including 18 780 between 8 and 14 November. Lahj and Taiz were the main destinations for those displaced between these dates.
Frontlines have moved through Lahj towards Aden, threatening referral routes and medical supply chains serving key hospitals, placing further pressure on an already overstretched health system. In Taiz, severe shortages of fuel, surgical supplies and anaesthesia medicines are disrupting emergency services, operating theatres and oxygen generation for intensive care units. Al-Mansoura General Surgical Hospital in Aden was receiving 15 to 20 people with conflict-related injuries each day when the interviews were conducted. For many of these patients, timely access to surgery and intensive care can mean the difference between life and death.
Already struggling with shortages of health workers, medical supplies and equipment, the hospital is working around the clock to meet the growing demand for emergency trauma care while continuing to provide essential services to patients with other urgent and chronic conditions.
With funding from the United Nations Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF), the World Health Organization (WHO), in coordination with the Ministry of Public Health and Population, is supporting a specialized surgical team working alongside hospital staff. CERF funding is also enabling WHO to deploy specialized surgical teams to other hospitals in Aden, Abyan and Taiz, helping expand access to lifesaving trauma and surgical services.
“We receive between 15 and 20 people with war injuries every day, and our department performs five to six operations daily,” says Dr Mustafa Mohammed Munassar, Head of Orthopaedics at Al-Mansoura General Surgical Hospital. “The number of wounded arriving at the hospital exceeds its capacity and the current staff.”
Surgical care involves more than the performing of operations. Patients need diagnostic examinations, anaesthesia, medicines, nursing care and monitoring during recovery. Shortages of funding and personnel are making it difficult for the hospital to meet these needs.
The pressure extends to intensive care units, where shortages of trained personnel prevent hospitals from fully using their available resources. Al-Mansoura Hospital has two intensive care units, one with six beds, the other with four. Staffing constraints mean that only the six-bed unit can be used.
“We need medical staff – nurses and doctors – so that we can open the second care unit,” says Dr Ahmed Mohammed Saeed Salem, Head of the Intensive Care Unit.
Without a CT scanner, patients – many of them in critical condition and unable to be easily moved – must be transferred elsewhere for diagnostic examinations. Surgical specialties share a single C-arm imaging device, and shortages of laboratory supplies and essential treatments further compound the challenges facing medical teams.
There is an urgent need for sustained support that combines specialized personnel, essential medical supplies and functioning equipment to ensure patients receive comprehensive care.
WHO support – including the provision of fuel, medical supplies, intravenous fluids and equipment, is helping hospital teams maintain essential services despite the pressures, says Dr Ahmed, and CERF-funded specialized surgical teams are reinforcing the capacity of hospitals to respond to urgent trauma cases.
Among the patients receiving care at Al-Mansoura Hospital was 18-year-old Abdullah Waddah, who needed emergency surgery after a road accident. His experience highlights the importance of maintaining care for everyday emergencies alongside the response to conflict-related injuries.
“The surgery was successful and everything is fine, praise be to God,” he says. “Our brothers the nurses did their best.”
During a visit to the hospital, WHO Representative in Yemen Dr Syed Jaffar Hussain met patients from Taiz and other areas affected by fighting. He highlighted the growing burden on health facilities which must treat people injured in the conflict while continuing to provide care for acute and chronic illnesses in the surrounding communities and displaced populations. As the conflict continues to place additional demands on Yemen's already strained health system, maintaining access to emergency surgical and critical care is essential.
Through CERF funding, WHO is working with national health authorities and health workers to keep lifesaving surgical services available to people affected by the conflict. Sustained investment will be critical to ensuring that hospitals can continue treating the wounded and providing essential care to communities whose needs are growing.
Thanking CERF for its support, Dr Hussain called for continued donor assistance to help health partners sustain the emergency response. “We will be able to save precious lives if we have the means,” he says.

Countries: Syrian Arab Republic, Lebanon
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Syria continues to witness large-scale returns of refugees and internally displaced persons (IDPs), alongside persistent humanitarian vulnerabilities and reintegration needs. Since December 2024, more than 1.8 million refugees and 2 million IDPs have returned. Meanwhile, 15.6 million people continue to require humanitarian assistance.

As returns continue, access to documentation, adequate housing, essential services, livelihoods and community support remains critical to ensuring sustainable reintegration and supporting Syria’s recovery.

In line with Syria’s National Recovery Priorities and the Government’s “No Tents, No Camps” vision, UNHCR supports return and reintegration efforts while continuing to provide protection and humanitarian assistance to vulnerable populations.

items.author: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
items.content:
Country: Zimbabwe
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Please refer to the attached file.

Description of the crisis

The cholera outbreak in Zimbabwe began on February 12, 2023, in the town of Chegutu, in Mashonaland West Province. The outbreak escalated quickly, with the first confirmed cases reported shortly after the initial outbreak date. By mid-January 2024, the situation peaked, with over 350 cases recorded in a single day. By mid-May 2024, the number of cases had dropped significantly to single digits, indicating a possible containment of the outbreak. The outbreak affected all 10 provinces of Zimbabwe and extended beyond traditional cholera hotspots to areas previously considered safe from cholera

Total cases: By early June 2024, approximately 34,518 cholera cases had been reported, with a cumulative death toll of 715, resulting in a case fatality rate (CFR) of approximately 2.0%.

items.title: World: UNHCR Global Appeal 2027
items.author: UN High Commissioner for Refugees
items.content:
Countries: World, Burkina Faso, Central African Republic, Chad, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Lebanon, Mali, Myanmar, Niger, Nigeria, South Sudan, Sudan, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

High Commissioner’s Foreword

In my first year as High Commissioner for Refugees, I have visited 15 countries. I have witnessed the desperation of people forced to flee conflict and persecution, and the immense pressures facing the countries and communities that welcome them. But I have also met people determined to rebuild their lives, contribute to their communities, and shape their own futures.

These experiences have reinforced my conviction that displacement must not define a person’s life. Our responsibility does not end when people find safety. We must also help create the conditions for them to rebuild their lives and find lasting solutions.

Our Strategic Directions for 2027-2031 set a clear course for this work. They establish four interconnected priorities: safeguarding international protection, advancing solutions, strengthening emergency preparedness and response, and advancing agency, inclusion and self-reliance. Protection remains the foundation of everything we do: safeguarding the right to asylum, upholding non-refoulement and enabling people to exercise their rights. We will strengthen our capacity to prepare for and respond rapidly and decisively to emergencies, while laying the foundations for longer-term solutions from the outset. We will pursue voluntary, safe and dignified return when conditions allow, alongside local integration, resettlement and complementary pathways.

We will also expand opportunities for refugees to exercise agency over their own lives and become more self-reliant through inclusion in national systems and services, access to employment, entrepreneurship and education, enabling them to contribute to the communities in which they live and help shape their own futures.

Our 50 by 35 vision gives this ambition a measurable goal: to halve by 2035 the number of refugees in protracted displacement who are dependent on humanitarian assistance. Around 14.5 million refugees currently live in such situations. Our vision is not about reducing humanitarian assistance but to reduce the need for it by enabling refugees to become more self-reliant, and by advancing lasting solutions. The 50 by 35 Accelerator will help turn this vision into action by mobilizing additional financing and technical support to address barriers to inclusion and unlock investment for refugees and host communities.

Delivering on these priorities in a fast-changing world demands change within the Agency. UNHCR is strongly committed to wider reform efforts under UN80 and the Humanitarian Reset. We are reshaping how we work, sharpening our focus in areas where we are best positioned to act, making more deliberate choices about operational presence, simplifying processes, reducing duplication and directing expertise and resources where they can have the greatest impact. We are also strengthening the way we work with others, with around one third of programme activities planned for delivery through partners. The objective is a transformed UNHCR: more agile, more focused on impact and results, more ready to partner with others, more transparent and accountable, more driven by data and innovation.

At its 77th session, UNHCR’s Executive Committee approved our 2027 programme budget of $7.137 billion. The resources available to deliver this programme will depend on donor contributions. As UNHCR and the wider humanitarian and development sector transform, the way we fund our work matters as much as the amount. However, the share of tightly earmarked contributions rose from 19% in 2022 to 51% in 2026, making it harder to respond quickly, sustain essential protection activities and direct resources where they are most needed.

We will therefore continue to appeal to donors to secure the greatest possible flexibility in funding.

Alongside humanitarian funding, we will work with governments, development institutions, and the private sector to mobilize investment in livelihoods, inclusive national systems and longer-term solutions. Such investment is essential to expanding opportunities and strengthening resilience, but it must complement, never replace, the resources needed for immediate protection and assistance.

The Global Compact on Refugees calls for responsibility-sharing that matches the leadership of refugee-hosting countries with sustained political, financial, and technical support. This will be essential to realizing our 50 by 35 vision. The Global Refugee Forum in December 2027 must turn these commitments into concrete action. Lasting solutions ultimately depend on peace and political action to address the causes of displacement. Humanitarian assistance can and must save lives, but it cannot solve the conflicts that force people from their homes. No refugee situation should become permanent simply because the world has grown accustomed to it.

I am deeply grateful to the governments, institutions, private donors, and individuals who provide consistent support to UNHCR. Your trust carries a responsibility to use resources wisely, demonstrate results honestly, and remain focused on the people we serve.

The choices we make today will shape the future of millions of people forced to flee. With sustained investment, collective resolve and political action to address the causes of displacement, we can protect and provide assistance to those in need, create opportunities for people to rebuild their lives, and advance lasting solutions. I invite you to join us in this effort.

items.title: Serbia moves to keep small businesses running when disaster strikes
items.author: UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction
items.content:
Country: Serbia
Source: UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction

Micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) are at the heart of Serbia's economy, accounting for 99% of all enterprises and, in 2024, more than 64% of employment and 56.9% of total gross value added. Yet they remain highly exposed to disaster risks, such as floods, fires, power outages, cyber-attacks and supply chain failures. These can disrupt operations, damage assets, cut revenues, and threaten livelihoods.

Through UNDRR’s Resilient Western Balkan initiative, financed by the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation (AICS), the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Serbia (CCIS) is helping MSMEs to build their disaster resilience and business continuity planning capacities. The initiative is developing a tailored package of MSME resilience tools and establishing a sustainable Business Continuity Advisory Service to train advisors nationwide to support MSMEs across the country.

A workshop held on 17 November in Belgrade brought businesses, ministries and international partners together to learn about the tools and process. Participants used the Resilience Maturity Assessment (ReMA) tool, developed by UNDRR and the Corporate Chief Resilience Officers (CCRO) network, to self-asses their businesses’ capacities to withstand disruptions and adapt to change. They also previewed the new Serbian-language package of guidelines and templates to support business continuity planning, aligned with UNDRR’s global guidance.

“MSMEs face particular challenges: limited capacity and know-how, no systematic financial support for building resilience, dependence on critical infrastructure, and increasingly complex market and supply chain requirements, especially for climate and cyber resilience,” said Vidosava Džagić, Assistant Director of the Chamber of Commerce of Belgrade, CCIS. “With UNDRR’s support, CCIS will build advisory services across the chamber system to help micro and small enterprises in particular assess their resilience maturity and develop business continuity plans, using UNDRR guidelines and the ReMA tool, as well as good international practice. Sector guides and templates will come first for manufacturing, food production, and transport and logistics, followed by IT services. Businesses are ready to help test the tools so they fit Serbian practice, and want joint business continuity simulations to be organised with other MSMEs and the Sector for Emergency Management.”

A 2020 survey by the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Serbia (CCIS) and UNDRR highlighted gaps in MSMEs’ capacity and resources to address disaster risks. Nearly half of surveyed businesses had no business continuity plans, around 40% reported that a recent disruption had halted operations for more than a month, and only 9% reported recovering with the support of insurance. While awareness of disaster risk has grown since then, business continuity planning and risk awareness remain uneven.

Under Serbian law, enterprises are required to prepare a Protection and Rescue Plan to protect people and property during an emergency. The plans provide businesses with practical tools to identify threats, prepare for emergencies and protect employees and property. But even when staff and premises are unharmed, a business can suffer serious disruption. Keeping operations running during and after a disruption requires additional planning.

Business Continuity Plans build on these efforts by helping companies prepare for disruptions that could affect their daily operations by helping them to es anticipate disruptions, minimize operational downtime and financial losses, and recover faster.

The workshop served as a starting point. Feedback from participants will shape the permanent CCIS advisory service for MSMEs, identify focus sectors for dedicated guidance materials, and inform a broader policy dialogue among Serbia's resilience stakeholders.

About the Resilient Western Balkans Initiative

The “Strengthening Transboundary Collaboration, Disaster Risk Reduction Capacities and Early Warning Systems in the Western Balkans” initiative aims to enhance disaster and climate resilience in Albania, North Macedonia, and Serbia. The initiative is implemented by UNDRR and financed by the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation (AICS). By strengthening risk knowledge, governance, early warning systems, and transboundary collaboration, the three-year initiative (July 2025 – July 2028) seeks to protect lives, livelihoods, and infrastructure across the region.

items.title: World: Making resilience an executive priority: Defining the role of Chief Resilience Officer
items.author: UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction
items.content:
Country: World
Source: UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction

A new model job description developed by UNDRR and the Corporate Chief Resilience Officers Network, with input from professional recruiters, helps companies establish dedicated resilience leadership and strengthen their ability to anticipate, withstand and recover from disruptions.

As businesses face increasingly complex and interconnected risks, resilience can no longer be treated solely as a matter of crisis response or business continuity. It requires strategic leadership, co-ordination across business functions and clear accountability at the executive level.

To help companies put this into practice, the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR), the Corporate Chief Resilience Officers (CCRO) Network, with input from professional recruiters, have developed a model job description for the Chief Resilience Officer (CResO) role.

Convened by UNDRR, the CCRO Network brings together senior resilience leaders from multinational companies across different sectors to share expertise, promote risk-informed business decisions and advance corporate resilience.

The resource builds on the case for dedicated executive resilience leadership made in the May 2026 Harvard Business Review article The Case for Hiring a Chief Resilience Officer, which highlighted the fragmentation of responsibility for resilience across corporate functions.

Why companies need resilience leadership

Disruptions rarely affect just one part of a business. An extreme weather event, infrastructure failure, cyberattack or supply chain disruption can simultaneously affect operations, employees, suppliers and customers. Managing cascading impacts requires decisions that cut across organisational boundaries.

While companies may have established risk management, business continuity and crisis management functions, these do not necessarily provide an integrated approach to resilience. The Chief Resilience Officer is intended to bridge this gap, connecting strategic decisions, investment and operational capabilities across the organisation.

Mikael Balslev Rasmussen, Head of Global Security & Business Resilience at Maersk and a member of the CCRO Network, said:

“Most companies already have people responsible for managing individual risks across the business. What is often missing is someone with the mandate to connect the dots. A Chief Resilience Officer can help turn vertical efforts into a coherent strategy, provide insight into resilience maturity, and ensure that resilience is considered not only when a crisis strikes, but in everyday business decisions and in how we empower people and enable technology to integrate and collaborate. The Chief Resilience Officer can facilitate and lead these efforts while still ensuring that resilience remains everyone’s business.”

What does a Chief Resilience Officer do?

The Chief Resilience Officer provides strategic leadership to help companies anticipate, withstand, respond to, recover from and adapt to disruption.

Rather than replacing existing functions, the CResO co-ordinates efforts across risk management, operations, finance, technology, cyber security, sustainability, security and business continuity, while business and functional leaders retain responsibility for execution within their respective areas.

The model job description identifies responsibilities including developing an organisation-wide resilience strategy; identifying critical services and dependencies; integrating risk intelligence into business planning; strengthening crisis preparedness, continuity and recovery; and measuring resilience performance to inform investment and executive decisions.

A practical template for companies

Developed with input from CCRO Network members and professional recruiters, the template translates these responsibilities into a practical framework for defining the role, its executive competencies, reporting arrangements and performance expectations.

It is deliberately flexible. Companies can adapt the job title, scope, authority and reporting line to their sector, governance arrangements, operating model and regulatory obligations.

Dr. Abhilash Panda, Deputy Chief of the Intergovernmental Processes, Interagency Cooperation and Partnerships Branch at UNDRR said:

"When businesses are disrupted, the consequences extend far beyond their own operations. Workers, communities, supply chains and entire economies can be affected. Building resilience into corporate leadership is therefore not just good business practice; it is an essential part of reducing disaster risk and protecting development gains."

The resource supports UNDRR's efforts to promote risk-informed business decisions and strengthen private sector resilience, helping companies move from reacting to disruptions towards anticipating risks and investing in preparedness.

Building resilience into corporate leadership is therefore not just good business practice; it is an essential part of reducing disaster risk and protecting development gains."
The resource supports UNDRR's efforts to promote risk-informed business decisions and strengthen private sector resilience, helping companies move from reacting to disruptions towards anticipating risks and investing in preparedness.
